title: Eating Processed Food Every Day Raised Dementia Risk by 58 Per Cent. Your Dadi's Kitchen Was the Opposite.
excerpt: A Harvard study of 5,300 people over 10 years found that ultraprocessed foods drive cognitive decline. Traditional South Asian cooking may be the strongest defence diaspora families already have.
body:
The headline number from a new Harvard study is stark: people who eat ultraprocessed foods daily have a 58 per cent higher risk of developing dementia. Over 10 years of tracking more than 5,300 Americans, researchers also found a 46 per cent increase in mild cognitive impairment — the early warning stage that often precedes Alzheimer's and other dementias.

Processed meats were the worst offenders. Bacon, hot dogs, deli slices — the convenient fillings and quick-cook proteins that dominate American weeknight dinners — contributed most to cognitive decline. But the broader category included everything from packaged biscuits and chips to sweetened cereals and frozen ready meals.

"Just to say, 'Well, I don't eat all my calories from ultraprocessed foods, I'm safe' — it really shows there may not be a safe level," said Professor Cindy Leung, associate professor of public health nutrition at Harvard and a study co-author.

## The Flip Side Was Equally Powerful

The study's most actionable finding may not be about what harms but what protects. Participants who ate the most minimally processed whole foods were 41 per cent less likely to develop dementia. That is not a marginal effect. It is a near-halving of risk from food choices alone.

Ultraprocessed foods, as classified under the NOVA system used by the researchers, are products with ingredients rarely found in a home kitchen: emulsifiers, artificial flavours, preservatives, hydrogenated oils, high-fructose corn syrup. They are engineered for shelf life and convenience, not nutrition. Their defining feature is that they cannot be replicated by cooking.

The mechanisms are not fully mapped, but researchers point to chronic inflammation, gut microbiome disruption, insulin resistance, and oxidative stress — all of which are accelerated by ultraprocessed diets and all of which are linked to neurodegeneration.

## The Diaspora Diet Problem

For South Asian families in America, this study lands in a complicated space. The traditional Indian kitchen — built on dal, sabzi, roti, rice, dahi, fresh chutneys, and whole spices — is almost entirely composed of minimally processed foods. Turmeric, cumin, coriander, mustard seeds, and ginger are not just flavour agents; they carry anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties that research has increasingly validated.

But the generational drift is real. Second-generation South Asian Americans grow up eating school lunches, packaged snacks, fast food, and the same convenience products as everyone else. First-generation parents, stretched between long work hours and cultural expectations, increasingly substitute frozen parathas, instant noodles, and packaged namkeen for the from-scratch cooking their own parents practised.

The data is personal. South Asians already carry elevated risks for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome — conditions that share inflammatory and insulin-resistant pathways with dementia. Adding ultraprocessed foods on top of a genetic predisposition creates a compounding risk that this Harvard study makes harder to dismiss.

## What the Data Suggests You Should Actually Do

The study does not call for perfection. It calls for direction. The researchers found that even partial substitution — replacing some ultraprocessed foods with whole, minimally processed alternatives — was associated with lower dementia risk.

For diaspora families, this is not a radical lifestyle overhaul. It is a return. Cooking dal from scratch instead of opening a can. Choosing fresh fruit over packaged fruit snacks. Making chutney from coriander and mint instead of buying bottled sauce with 14 ingredients. These are not novel interventions. They are the habits that a generation of grandmothers practised without knowing the science behind them.

The strongest defence against cognitive decline may already be sitting in the spice box. The question is whether the next generation will use it.
